scoreNote: Strong (5): a recommendation-appropriate response that shows where long-term goals beat the pursuit of fame and then carefully qualifies the word 'realistic' so it does not stifle ambition; concrete and persuasive.

sentences.text: In an age when a single video can make an unknown teenager famous overnight, the pull of instant recognition has never been stronger.
Against it, the recommendation urges young people to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than chase immediate fame.

The recommendation is largely wise, because lasting fulfillment grows from sustained effort rather than from sudden celebrity, though the word realistic should not be used to discourage genuine ambition.

sections.role: Body — Long-term goals build something real

sentences.text: First, long-term goals build the skills, character, and satisfaction that fleeting fame cannot.
Mastery of anything worthwhile — medicine, music, a craft, a science — takes years of patient work, and the person who pursues it gains abilities that remain when the applause fades.
A young woman who spends a decade becoming an excellent surgeon has built something no viral moment could give her and nothing a scandal could take away.
Fulfillment tends to come from growth and contribution, not from being noticed, and a life organized around recognition is built on the shifting opinions of strangers.
Long-term goals also teach resilience, since they are reached only by surviving the setbacks that a quick path never encounters.
Skills compound quietly over years, while fame, even when it lands, can evaporate within a week.
What is earned slowly tends to last; what arrives overnight tends to vanish overnight.

sections.role: Body — Fame is hollow and unreliable

sentences.text: Moreover, immediate fame is both unreliable as a goal and hollow as a reward.
Fame arrives, when it arrives at all, by luck as much as merit, so to aim at it is to stake one's life on a lottery.
For every young person made briefly famous online, countless others chase the same recognition and gain nothing but wasted years.
Those who do achieve sudden fame often find it empty, fleeting, and corrosive, since attention is not the same as respect and rarely satisfies for long.
The modern machinery of instant celebrity is especially treacherous, rewarding spectacle over substance and discarding people as fast as it raises them.
Aiming at applause means letting strangers decide whether your life has succeeded.
To build a life around so fickle a prize is to build on sand.

sections.role: Body — But do not let 'realistic' kill ambition

sentences.text: However, the recommendation must be read with care, because the word realistic can do real harm.
Told to be realistic, a gifted young person might abandon a bold dream — to start a company, make art, change a field — that looked impossible but was well worth attempting.
The point is not to aim low but to aim at something real and lasting rather than at mere visibility.
A long-term goal can be wildly ambitious, even unlikely, as long as it is pursued for its substance and not for the spotlight.
There is a world of difference between a hard dream and a hollow one.
In conclusion, young people are well advised to pursue long-term goals over immediate fame.
Sustained effort toward something real builds skill, resilience, and genuine fulfillment, while the chase for instant recognition usually delivers neither and rarely lasts.
Aim high and aim far, and let any fame that comes arrive as the reward for the work rather than as its purpose.
